The finely brushed dial is equally restrained, with a small seconds display at 6 o'clock. Applied hour markers and faceted Dauphine hands echo the historic original, creating a look that is both refined and timeless. The strap, created by Argentine leather specialist Casa Fagliano, further reinforces the watch's unique blend of elegance and sporting heritage. Inside beats a manually wound movement that perfectly suits the watch's minimalist character. By dispensing with unnecessary complications, the Reverso focuses on the essentials, a reminder of why it remains one of the most distinctive and enduring designs in modern watchmaking. World Time Instead of GMT: Omega – Seamaster Aqua Terra 150M Worldtimer Omega proves that technical sophistication and everyday practicality can go hand in hand with the Seamaster Aqua Terra 150M Worldtimer. Priced at $11,200, Ref. 220.10.43.22.03.001 combines the sporty elegance of the Aqua Terra collection with one of modern watchmaking's most compelling complications: a true world time display. The 43mm stainless-steel case has a confident wrist presence yet remains surprisingly wearable thanks to its balanced proportions. The dial is the undisputed centerpiece. At its heart sits a three-dimensional titanium representation of the Earth, created using laser ablation to sculpt the continents and oceans in remarkable detail. Surrounded by a city ring displaying the world's major time zones, allowing all 24 time zones to be read simultaneously. Despite the wealth of information, the dial remains impressively legible. Shades of blue, intricate textures, and a carefully balanced layout give the watch a distinctly modern, technical aesthetic while preserving the Aqua Terra's signature blend of sporty versatility and maritime inspiration. Powering the watch is Omega's Master Chronometer Caliber 8938, certified by METAS to the highest standards of precision, magnetic resistance, and reliability. The automatic movement delivers a 60-hour power reserve, resists magnetic fields up to 15,000 gauss, and features a Co-Axial escapement, a silicon balance spring, and an independently adjustable local-hour hand, ideal for frequent travelers. Eye-catcher: Ming x J.N. Shapiro – 37.06 Lightning The Ming × J.N. Shapiro 37.06 Lightning is one of the most remarkable collaborations to emerge from independent watchmaking in recent years. Created by two members of the Alternative Horological Alliance, it combines Ming's unmistakable design language with Josh Shapiro's traditional guilloché craftsmanship. The result is a watch whose dial is not simply decorated, it is painstakingly created. Each dial begins as a solid titanium blank, hand-engine-turned in Los Angeles on a century-old rose engine. The resulting Lightning Guilloché pattern creates a dramatic texture that appears to shift and flow as the light changes. The dial then travels to Kuala Lumpur, where Ming founder Ming Thein personally heat-treats it with an open flame. Carefully controlled temperatures produce iridescent shades of blue, violet, bronze, and gold, without paints, coatings, or chemical treatments. Because both the guilloché work and the heat coloring involve exceptionally high rejection rates, no two dials are ever alike. Every watch is effectively one of a kind. The familiar 38mm stainless-steel case from Ming's 37 Series provides the perfect stage for this visual spectacle. A slim bezel, dramatically domed sapphire crystal, and HyCeram hour markers embedded within the crystal further enhance the dial's remarkable sense of depth. Inside beats the hand-wound Caliber SW210.M1, exclusively finished for Ming and offering a power reserve of approximately 42 hours. Part work of art, part wristwatch, the 37.06 Lightning is priced at CHF 6,250, approximately $7,800. This article was first published by WatchTime Germany.

title: Dawesome launches Abyss II synthesizer built for musicians
description:
Dawesome has released the next evolution of its color-based synthesizer for Windows and Mac (VST3, AU and AAX). Abyss II aims to transform how musicians create signature textures, pads, and evolving soundscapes by replacing traditional oscillator menus with pure timbral exploration. Warm, cold, dark, brilliant, silky, lush … we use the exact same words to [...]

The post Dawesome launches Abyss II synthesizer built for musicians appeared first on Rekkerd.org.
content: Dawesome has released the next evolution of its color-based synthesizer for Windows and Mac (VST3, AU and AAX). Abyss II aims to transform how musicians create signature textures, pads, and evolving soundscapes by replacing traditional oscillator menus with pure timbral exploration. Warm, cold, dark, brilliant, silky, lush … we use the exact same words to describe sounds as we use to describe colours. This simple yet radical premise forms the heart of the instrument: sound is processed by our brains just like colour and texture. By throwing out abstract formulas, numbers, and tech jargon, the synth offers a purely intuitive playground where sound design feels like messing with paint. Most synthesizers force musicians to think like engineers. Abyss II is designed for pure creative flow: pick tone colours, place them on a visual gradient, and shape your sound by pure instinct. Abyss II features - Feed It Anything: Drop any sound into Abyss II – from a phone voice recording of a distant crane to a guitar snippet. The engine instantly extracts its unique timbral character, tunes it automatically, and creates visual “Palettes” of tone colours to draw from. - Pure Flow, Endless Variety: Combine multiple tone colours on a single gradient, or explore thousands of built-in colours to create your own unique expressive instruments. - Instant Character: the performance controls allow musicians to simply add character. New in Abyss II are BRUTE, VELVET and SYNTIFY, which do exactly what their name says. - Creative FX chain: A custom chain of four effect slots with 20 unique “pedals” to effortlessly shape your sonic character. - Kinetik & Movement: An integrated poly-rhythmic sequencer with independent step lengths for pitch, octave, gate, and velocity brings static sounds to life with endless, non-repeating movement. - 400+ presets: 200+ new designed presets and 200+ upgraded classics from Abyss 1. - Workflow & QoL Upgrades: mono-synth mode, a full-featured preset browser with tags and favs, a preset name generator, undo/redo, wave-drag-out of recently played notes, light on CPU usage. Abyss II is on sale for the intro price of $89 USD for a limited time (regular $149 USD). Owners of Abyss 1 can upgrade for $45 USD during the promotion (regular $75 USD). Anyone who purchased the original Abyss in 2026 receives the upgrade to Abyss II completely free. A free full-featured demo version is available to try the plugin. Abyss II is available to purchase at the Tracktion store and from distributors such as AudioDeluxe and Plugin Boutique.

title: Glashütte Original Senator Chronograph and Navigator Debut for 2026
description: Glashütte Original introduces the Senator Chronograph and Senator Chronograph Navigator with 41mm cases, flyback movements, and 70-hour power reserves.
content: Glashütte Original Senator Chronograph and Navigator Debut for 2026 Two takes on Glashütte chronograph history Glashütte Original today expands its Senator collection with the new Senator Chronograph and Senator Chronograph Navigator, two 41mm flyback chronographs built around the same case and movement, with distinct, historically-inspired dials. Founded in the Saxon watchmaking town of Glashütte, the manufacture has long built its identity around traditional German watchmaking, with the Senator collection serving as one of its clearest expressions of that approach. The line has encompassed everything from simple three-hand watches to more elaborate calendar and chronograph complications, typically framed through restrained, classically minded design. The Senator line is no stranger to the chronograph. Previous models have included the Senator Chronograph Panorama Date, though this latest pair takes the complication in a slimmer and more historically driven direction. That approach also connects back to a much longer chronograph tradition in Glashütte, including the UROFA Calibre 59 developed in the early 1940s, which the brand describes as the first modern Glashütte wristwatch chronograph. The new models draw from two sides of that history. The Senator Chronograph Navigator looks to mid-century pilot's watches, while the standard Senator Chronograph takes its cues from the precision observation watches once used for maritime navigation in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Despite their different personalities, both watches use the same 41mm stainless-steel case, measuring 12.9mm thick and 48.5mm from lug to lug. Sapphire crystals sit front and back, while water resistance is rated to 5 bar, or 50m. Mushroom-style chronograph pushers sit at 2 and 4 o'clock, with a tachymeter scale running around the dial’s rehaut. The Navigator adds a larger pilot-style crown, a small functional detail that helps reinforce its more utilitarian character. The Senator Chronograph Navigator is the sportier of the two, with Its matte black dial drawing directly from Glashütte pilot's watches of the 1940s. The look pairs luminous Arabic numerals with Super-LumiNova-coated hour and minute hands. The central chronograph seconds hand, 30-minute counter hand, and small seconds hand are finished in white lacquer, keeping the display highly legible against the dark dial. The standard Senator Chronograph takes a more formal approach, drawing inspiration from observation watches produced in Glashütte during the late 19th and early 20th centuries — namely precision pocket watches of the time used for maritime navigation. That influence comes through in a silver-white grainé dial with blue-coated solid-gold Roman numerals and blued hands. The 30-minute counter and small seconds sit opposite one another, while Glashütte Original's Panorama Date anchors the layout at 6 o'clock within a white-gold frame. Inside both watches is the automatic Calibre 37-24, an integrated column-wheel flyback chronograph movement combining central chronograph seconds, a 30-minute counter, small seconds, and the Panorama Date. The flyback function allows the chronograph to be stopped, reset, and restarted in a single operation, while the movement runs at 4 Hz and delivers a 70-hour power reserve. A silicon balance spring adds resistance to magnetic fields and temperature changes, with gold regulating screws and Glashütte Original's swan-neck fine adjustment handling regulation. Visible through the sapphire caseback, the Calibre 37-24 is finished with beveled edges, polished steel components, blued screws, and a three-quarter plate with Glashütte stripes. A newly developed skeletonized rotor incorporates a 21-carat gold oscillating weight. Both the Senator Chronograph and Senator Chronograph Navigator are offered on Louisiana alligator leather, a sand-colored synthetic strap, or a stainless-steel bracelet. The straps use a tool-free quick-change system, and the folding clasp can also be transferred between straps using a new quick-change mechanism. The watches are available worldwide through Glashütte Original boutiques and authorized retailers. U.S. pricing is marked at $16,100 on leather or textile straps and $17,100 on the stainless-steel bracelet.

title: H. Moser & Cie. Launches the Endeavour Minute Repeater Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Cosmic Rain
description: The H. Moser & Cie. Endeavour Minute Repeater Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Cosmic Rain combines a minute repeater, a flying tourbillon, and an artistic aventurine dial in a limited edition of 20 pieces.
content: H. Moser & Cie. Launches the Endeavour Minute Repeater Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Cosmic Rain A horological ménage à trois Reaching for the Stars With the Endeavour Minute Repeater Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Cosmic Rain, H. Moser & Cie. unites three of haute horlogerie’s most demanding complications and disciplines in a single timepiece. The titanium watch is equipped with a minute repeater, a fully skeletonized manufacture movement, and a rare flying tourbillon with a cylindrical hairspring. Completing the composition is an intricately crafted aventurine sub dial with mother-of-pearl marquetry that evokes the appearance of shimmering stars across the night sky. A Minute Repeater in Full View The minute repeater takes center stage — but not in the usual way. Traditionally positioned on different levels, the gongs are here integrated on a single plane, a true technical feat demanding extreme precision in their shaping, alignment, and tuning. Volumes are meticulously recalibrated, and every component refined for both performance and visibility. The hollowed titanium case is conceived as a resonance chamber, amplifying and sustaining each vibration. The result is a chime that is both precise and expressive. While the sound is music to enthusiasts' ears, the intricate choreography of the mechanism is every bit as captivating to the eye. This unconventional construction required a complete redesign of the hand-wound Caliber HMC 909. Comprising 415 individual components, the movement beats at 21,600 vibrations per hour and offers a power reserve of 90 hours. Extensive skeletonization opens up the bridges and mainplate, revealing the movement's layered design and emphasizing the intricate choreography of its mechanical components. The intricate beauty of the caliber can be admired through both the dial and the sapphire crystal case back. A Rare Cylindrical Hairspring Positioned at 6 o'clock, the flying one-minute tourbillon is equipped with one of watchmaking's rarest regulating organs: a cylindrical hairspring. Originally developed for precision marine chronometers in the 18th century, the hairspring coils vertically around the balance staff rather than expanding in a flat plane, improving concentric breathing and supporting more consistent timekeeping. Each cylindrical hairspring is handcrafted by Precision Engineering AG, H. Moser & Cie.'s sister company, using highly specialized manufacturing techniques that only a handful of companies still master today. A Starry Sky in Aventurine Providing a striking contrast to the open mechanics is the small domed hours-and-minutes sub dial positioned at 2 o'clock. Crafted from aventurine glass, it features H. Moser & Cie.'s signature fumé effect. Fragments of differently colored aventurine are applied by hand and fired several times before fine strips of mother-of-pearl are inlaid into the engraved surface. The result resembles a shower of stars crossing the night sky, giving the watch its "Cosmic Rain" designation and adding an artistic dimension to its highly technical character. Titanium for Better Acoustics The Endeavour Minute Repeater Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Cosmic Rain has its entrance in a 40mm case crafted from titanium and measuring 14.4mm in height. Beyond its lightweight properties, titanium was selected for its excellent acoustic performance, helping to enhance both the volume and clarity of the minute repeater. The striking mechanism is activated via a slide on the left side of the case. Limited to 20 pieces worldwide, the watch is paired with a hand-stitched gray nubuck alligator leather strap secured by a titanium pin buckle. Pricing is available on request.

title: Watch Week Aspen 2026 Wraps Its Biggest Edition Yet
description: The third annual gathering brought more than 300 attendees to Aspen for four days of watches, collector events, and outdoor programming, with WatchTime joining as an event partner.
content: Watch Week Aspen 2026 Wraps Its Biggest Edition Yet A weekend of watches in the Rockies Watch Week Aspen returned to Colorado last weekend for its third and largest edition yet, bringing more than 300 attendees to downtown Aspen for four days of new watches, collector gatherings, educational programming, and outdoor events. Co-founded by Oliver Smith Jeweler, Watch Week Aspen takes a different approach from the traditional watch fair, spreading its programming across boutiques, galleries, hotels, and public spaces rather than concentrating everything under one roof. This year's edition included 40 events and a record 19 participating watch brands, retailers, and industry partners. WatchTime joined this year as an official event partner. At Oliver Smith Jeweler, WatchTime moderated "In Conversation: The Independent Revolution," featuring Moritz Grossmann Founder and CEO Christine Hutter, George Reid, Director of Fine Timepieces, and Cyrus Watches' Mirko Bertolucci. The panel looked at the growing collector interest around independent watchmaking and where the category goes next. WatchTime also took part in the closing Collector's Dinner at W Aspen, joining guests for watch trivia and a friendly collector competition. New Watches and Brand Highlights Several brands used the weekend to unveil new pieces. Norqain debuted its Independence Skeleton Titanium DLC at Oliver Smith Jeweler, while Glashütte Original and L. Leroy each introduced new watches during their respective events. Elsewhere, A. Lange & Söhne brought its "Lumen" collection, Hermès offered a closer look at the mechanics and thinking behind Le temps suspendu, and Meridian Jewelers presented new and rare pieces from IWC. Omega focused on the Speedmaster, Buccellati showed watches from its Macri and Tulle collections, and Avi & Co. brought a selection of new and rare pieces. Arnold & Son, Blancpain, Cyrus Watches, Gerald Charles, and Moritz Grossmann were among the other participating brands, while Avi & Co., Betteridge, Meridian Jewelers, M.S. Rau, and Oliver Smith Jeweler joined as retail partners. Beyond the Boutique As in previous editions, plenty of the weekend happened outside the usual watch-show setting. Norqain hosted the first Watch Week Aspen 3K Run, led by U.S. Brand President Emmanuel Bütler, before following it with the brand's "Enjoy Life" ice cream truck activation. Gerald Charles hosted a three-day collector lounge at Oliver Smith Jeweler, then took guests to the courts for tennis and pickleball. Analog:Shift and Betteridge debuted VintageFest, giving collectors a place to bring out favorite vintage watches and spend some time around historic pieces. The social side of the weekend included the Golden Hour Welcome Party from Blancpain and Betteridge, SYYNCH's "State of the Market" gathering, and an evening of watches, cocktails, and canapés hosted by Avi & Co. There was plenty of more traditional watchmaking programming, too. L. Leroy CEO Hugo Lesizza presented the Maison's latest creations alongside a tasting from Accendo Estate, Christine Hutter hosted an afternoon focused on German watchmaking, and Arnold & Son closed the weekend with its latest collection. M.S. Rau also hosted a four-part series covering complications, unconventional design, fine watchmaking, and vintage and pre-owned watches. Three years in, Watch Week Aspen is starting to feel less like a regional watch gathering and more like a destination event, with serious collector access wrapped into a weekend that could only really happen in Aspen.

title: Blast from the Past: A Vintage Spotlight on the Gérald Genta Retro
description: A closer look at the Gérald Genta Retro Sport, a watch that reflects its creator’s most personal ideas, from jump hours and retrograde minutes to a design language rooted in technical daring rather than nostalgia.
content: Blast from the Past: A Vintage Spotlight on the Gérald Genta Retro A closer look at the Gérald Genta Retro Sport Gérald Genta is a name that needs no introduction. It is as legendary as the watches he designed, which says quite something as he is the creative father of both the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak and Patek Philippe’s Nautilus as well as many more. While very successfully designing for others, Genta’s creative force was so strong that he needed more to express himself, and he founded his own brand in 1969 to do just that. There he went on to not only design but also build watches that themselves would earn a well-respected status in the industry. Among them are his highly complex Sonnerie models, but also the Gefica, which he innovated with bronze cases long before they became popular, and the highly regarded Retro. The name Retro has no relation to reliving past times or the way things were. As a designer, Genta was always very forward focused and never lost himself in romantic reinterpretations of the past. For this collection, “Retro” stood for retrograde, which was, together with the jumping hour, one of its main features. From a technical point of view, a jump hour and a retrograde minute (later models even included a retrograde date as well) are quite challenging to make. This comes from the fact that both are quite volatile mechanisms in which, for an entire hour, energy has to be stored, only to be released in a split second when the minute hand jumps back to its starting position and the hour disk jumps forward. Here, it is important for the hour disk to remain perfectly aligned, as the numerals are quite large, and even the smallest deviation will be noticeable. Given Genta’s extensive expertise with these devices, the dependability of this is ensured. For that, he also opted for a reliable base movement, the ETA 2892-A2, providing plenty of power for the module that transforms this regular three-hand movement into a jump hour with retrograde minutes. As a designer, displaying time this way gave Genta a unique freedom that he really seized. While this is most prominently shown in the Retro models that incorporated Disney figures, it is also present in a slightly more subtle way in this Retro Sport. Its more sportive nature than its sibling, the Retro Classic, resonates from a combination of details. One of the most beautiful is the way Genta sculpted the crown guards from the side of the case. It is a perfect symbiosis of form and function that also organically integrates it into the design of the rest of the watch. The Retro Sport has a slightly larger diameter than the Retro Classic, 40 mm compared to 38 mm. The polished and domed bezel sets the stage for a very interesting dial that is not only extremely legible but also full of details. This starts with the woven carbon fiber at the dial’s center. It is subtle, even refined, yet undeniably sportive. The matte ring surrounding it features Gérald Genta’s brand name in relief at the top, flanking the polished window outline for the jump hour display. The bottom half is used for the minute indications in bold Arabic numerals. The 10-minute increments are filled with Super-LumiNova, as are the minute hand and the dots with the 5-minute increments printed in white. This makes reading the time in the dark also quite easy, as the Super-LumiNova is applied quite thickly. This is also done with the hour numerals, but as they are underneath the dial before the start of “their” hour, they don’t change themselves until then. The changing of the hour comes with a nice clicking sound, and although no bell is hit, it can function for its owner as a “sonnerie au passage.” The dial is surrounded by a ring indicating the seconds, a function that also sets the Retro Sport apart from the Retro Classic. This ring is placed slightly higher, adding to the depth of the dial. Both the minute and the seconds hand are blued. This means that the seconds hand remains under most angles hidden above the dark colors of the dial, except its top, which is painted in red. When light hits the hands at the right angle, flashes of blue confirm that this Retro Sport is an extraordinary watch. It is also a watch that is easy to live with. The proportions are not overly generous, making it feel at home even on a more modestly sized wrist. The short lugs also help with this, securing the strap with a screw-in pin for added security. The caseback is also secured by screws, six in total, and decorated quite soberly. That is good because it makes the engraved Retro Sport logo stand out even more, while it also sits nice and flat on the wrist. Gérald Genta made this Retro Sport in the first years of the new millennium. It was priced in those days at $5,300, making it quite an exclusive offering, yet on par with its original nature and high build quality. While Genta’s name will forever be connected with some of the most legendary watches ever designed, it was his own brand that was his home where he could do as he pleased. That makes watches such as this Retro Sport perhaps his most personal expression and an insight into a brilliant mind and skilled hand. This article was originally published in the January / February Issue. To subscribe to the print edition of WatchTime Magazine, click here.

title: Armin Strom Gives the Mirrored Force Resonance a Bold Red Dial
description: The independent Biel-based manufacture gives the Mirrored Force Resonance a vivid red hand-guilloché dial while retaining its patented twin-balance resonance system and hand-wound ARF21 caliber.
content: Armin Strom Gives the Mirrored Force Resonance a Bold Red Dial Two oscillators, one rhythm, and a lot more color A New Look for a Signature Timepiece Armin Strom is giving one of its most technically sophisticated watches a fresh new appearance. The Mirrored Force Resonance Red joins the collection with a vibrant red dial while retaining the resonance technology that has become one of the independent Biel-based manufacture’s defining innovations since its debut in 2016. The asymmetrical display divides the dial into two distinct areas. On the right, the off-center time display features a hand-guilloché pattern created on a traditional rose engine. The radiating motif enhances the vivid red color, which changes in intensity depending on the light. A black azurage minute track and faceted, polished hour markers provide contrast and emphasize the dial’s depth. The Fascination of Resonance The left side of the watch is dedicated to the movement’s mechanical prowess. Here, two independent balance wheels oscillate side by side, connected by Armin Strom’s patented resonance clutch. As the balances exchange energy, they gradually synchronize and begin oscillating in resonance, improving rate stability. Twin small-seconds displays allow the wearer to observe the synchronized operation, while a pusher at 2 o’clock resets both seconds hands simultaneously. Two Oscillators, One Rhythm At the heart of the Mirrored Force Resonance Red beats the hand-wound manufacture Caliber ARF21, a movement that exemplifies Armin Strom's uncompromising approach to independent watchmaking. Rather than relying on a single regulating system, it incorporates two complete movements within one caliber, each with its own mainspring barrel, gear train, escapement, and balance wheel. The two systems communicate exclusively through the brand's patented resonance clutch, allowing them to synchronize naturally while enhancing rate stability. The movement operates at a frequency of 3.5 Hz (25,200 vibrations per hour) and offers a power reserve of 48 hours. Framed by sapphire crystals on both the front and back, the ARF21 reveals an architecture that is as captivating as its mechanics. Every component is finished by hand, with polished bevels, perlage, circular graining, and black-polished screws underscoring the high horological craftsmanship for which Armin Strom is renowned. The stainless-steel case measures 43mm in diameter and 11.55mm in height and is paired with a dark gray Alcantara strap with contrasting white stitching. The Mirrored Force Resonance Red is limited to 15 pieces worldwide and is priced at CHF 78,000 or approximately $96,063 when converted to USD.

title: The Best Mechanical Watches Under $1,000
description: Good mechanical watchmaking does not have to cost a fortune. These automatic and hand-wound models stand out for their distinctive design, dependable engineering, and thoughtful details.
content: The Best Mechanical Watches Under $1,000 Seven affordable watches to know The selection of mechanical watches available for less than $1,000 is broader and more diverse than ever. Alongside established manufacturers such as Citizen, Hamilton, and Laco, German brands and smaller independent companies are bringing fresh energy to the category. Circula, Sternglas, and Vandaag pursue distinctive design identities, while Venezianico gives traditional decorative techniques a surprisingly modern interpretation. Technical specifications and low prices alone were not enough to secure a place on this list. We looked for watches that succeed as complete packages, combining balanced proportions, practical everyday features, credible quality, and designs with lasting appeal. Only models powered by automatic or hand-wound movements and regularly available for less than $1,000 were considered. Sternglas: Naos Automatic Edition Bauhaus X With the Naos Edition Bauhaus X, Sternglas gives its familiar Bauhaus design a more experimental character. The essential architecture remains intact: a polished 38mm stainless-steel case, slender hands, and clean typography preserve the restrained aesthetic of the Naos. For the first time, however, the Hamburg-based brand equips the model with a fully luminous dial. In darkness, the glowing surface emerges behind the black applied markers, giving the geometric composition an unusual sense of depth. The edition is offered in the three primary Bauhaus colors: red, yellow, and blue. Each accent color appears on the seconds hand, the contrasting stitching of the black vintage leather strap, and the tinted exhibition window in the caseback. The result gives each version its own identity without disrupting the clarity of the design. A domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating on both sides protects the dial. A UV flashlight is also included, allowing the luminous material to be charged on demand. The automatic Miyota 8215 caliber is visible through the colored caseback. It offers manual winding, a stop-seconds function, a date display at 6 o’clock, and approximately 42 hours of power reserve. Each colorway is limited to 500 pieces and individually numbered on the caseback. References S02-NAI24-VI29 (Red), S02-NAI23-VI22 (Yellow), S02-NAI45-VI30 (Blue) | Stainless Steel 316L, 38 mm | Caliber Miyota 8215, Automatic | Power reserve: 42 hours | Water-resistant up to 50 m | Limited to 500 pieces per color | Approximately $560 Hamilton: Khaki Field Mechanical 36 mm The Hamilton Khaki Field Mechanical 36mm draws closely on the FAPD 5101, a navigation watch issued to U.S. Air Force crews around 1970. Rather than merely reproducing its appearance, Hamilton carries over many of the original’s functional details, including the fully matte stainless-steel case, fixed lugs, and domed acrylic crystal. Paired with a khaki cotton NATO strap, the result is a field watch with a convincingly authentic, understated tool-watch character. At 36mm, the case is compact even by current standards, though perfectly aligned with the ongoing return to smaller cases. Its elongated lugs provide sufficient wrist presence, while the slim 10.2mm profile should ensure a comfortable fit. The black dial remains faithful to the historical model, with a crisp minute track, Arabic numerals, and slender hands. Super-LumiNova Grade X2 improves legibility in low light. Power comes from the hand-wound Hamilton H-50 caliber, based on the ETA 2801-2, with an impressive 80-hour power reserve. A Nivachron hairspring reduces sensitivity to magnetic fields, temperature fluctuations, and shocks. Also noteworthy are the 100-meter water resistance and an additional dust cover. The Khaki Field Mechanical 36mm will be produced exclusively during 2026. Reference H69399930 | Stainless steel, 36mm | Caliber Hamilton H-50, hand-wound | Power reserve: 80 hours | Water resistance: 100 meters | Exclusively produced in 2026 | Approximately $770. Venezianico: Arsenale 40 With the Arsenale 40, Venezianico transfers a traditional movement-finishing technique to the dial. Instead of decorating bridges or plates, vertical Côtes de Genève animate the visible face of the watch. The effect is especially striking on Ref. 6221501C: depending on the light, its purple dial shifts between vivid and more subdued tones, while the parallel waves add visual depth. Skeletonized dauphine hands and slender applied markers keep the overall composition clean and restrained. The 40mm stainless-steel case is only 8.95mm high, including the sapphire crystal. Combined with a compact 44mm length and the integrated-style Canova Concept steel bracelet, the Arsenale is notably slim and compact. Brushed surfaces, polished bevels, and a finely textured bezel add definition to its sporty-elegant form. Inside works the slim automatic Miyota 9029 caliber with a 42-hour power reserve. The absence of both a date display and a seconds hand reinforces the watch’s calm, graphic character. In addition to purple, Venezianico offers the Arsenale 40 with a Côtes de Genève dial in blue and anthracite. Reference 6221501C | Stainless steel 316L, 40mm | Caliber Miyota 9029, automatic | Power reserve: 42 hours | Water resistance: 50 meters | Approximately $900. Citizen: Series 8 Positioned as a sporty-elegant mechanical collection within Citizen’s upper range, the Series 8 NB6080-51W combines distinctive design with everyday versatility, strong magnetic resistance, and compelling value. At just under 40mm, the stainless-steel case is suitably compact by contemporary standards, yet its angular construction, assembled from several carefully finished components, gives it considerable presence. Paired with an integrated-style stainless-steel bracelet, the watch moves easily between casual wear and business attire. The light green dial provides the strongest visual accent. Its finely structured pattern combines a stylized nighttime view of the Tokyo skyline with a traditional Japanese check motif. Applied hour markers and sharply defined hands ensure good legibility, while an anti-reflective sapphire crystal protects the dial. Inside works Citizen’s automatic manufacture Caliber 9051, engineered for enhanced magnetic resistance and visible through the sapphire caseback. It offers stop seconds, a date display, and a 42-hour power reserve. Water resistance to 10 bar further strengthens the NB6080-51W’s everyday credentials. At €895, Citizen delivers a thoughtfully designed and carefully finished automatic watch with an impressive price-to-performance ratio. Reference NB6080-51W | Stainless steel, 39.85mm | Caliber Citizen 9051, automatic | Power reserve: 42 hours | Water resistance: 100 meters | Approximately $1,000. Vandaag: Klaar The Vandaag Klaar is currently the brand’s best-selling model. Conceived as a sporty everyday watch, it is designed to accompany its wearer anywhere. The three-hand model offers strong legibility, a screw-down crown, and a unidirectional rotating bezel with a ceramic insert and 120-click action. Despite its restrained design, the bezel can still be used for timing, while the Klaar deliberately avoids an overt instrument aesthetic. The dark dial is available in black, gray, dark green, and dark blue, each contrasted by bright Arabic numerals. Red accents appear on the date display and around the tip of the central seconds hand. Nemoto luminous material on the hands and numerals ensures clear readability in varying light conditions and, depending on the version, emits a green glow in the dark. The 42.5mm stainless-steel case measures 11.65mm in height, excluding the domed sapphire crystal. With a lug-to-lug length of 50mm, it is not a small watch, though its comparatively slim case makes it flatter than the Schallmauer Automatic. The surfaces are predominantly brushed, while polished bevels along the lugs and lower case edge sharpen the contours. Vandaag selected the Sellita SW200-1 in Elaboré grade for the movement. The brand fits it with a custom black rotor and has the rate performance optimized by its own watchmaker. A screw-down caseback with a sapphire window leaves the movement visible. Production is limited to 300 pieces in each dial color. The three-link stainless-steel bracelet features screwed links, quick-release spring bars, and a folding clasp with twin pushers. Rubber straps are also available. Klaar Gold-Kraft | Stainless steel, 42.5mm | Caliber Sellita SW200-1, automatic | Power reserve: 42 hours | Water resistance: 100 meters | Approximately $1,000. Laco: Original Heidelberg Pilot Watch The Laco Original Heidelberg translates the design of the famous 1940 observation watch into a contemporary 39mm format. Its black dial follows the historic Type A layout, with large Arabic hour numerals, a clearly defined minute track, and the characteristic triangle flanked by two dots at 12 o’clock for instant orientation. Laco deliberately omits a brand logo, just as the original military instruments carried no manufacturer on the dial. The numerals, markers, and thermally blued steel hands are coated with Super-LumiNova C3. The 39mm stainless-steel case is dark sandblasted to minimize reflections. Straight lugs, an easy-to-grip crown, and the “FL 23883” engraving on the case flank reference further details of the historical models. A domed sapphire crystal with an anti-reflective coating on the underside combines period-correct styling with modern scratch resistance. The brown calfskin strap, finished with decorative rivets, complements the watch’s functional character. Despite its close historical ties, the Heidelberg remains well suited to everyday wear, with a 12.15mm height and water resistance to 10 bar. Inside works the automatic Laco 200 movement, based on the Sellita SW200-1. It comes standard in Elaboré grade, while a Top-grade version and additional decorative finishing are available at extra cost. Reference 862094 | Stainless steel, 39mm | Caliber Sellita SW200-1, automatic | Power reserve: 38 hours | Water resistance: 100 meters | Approximately $1,000. Circula: AquaSport II The Circula AquaSport II combines the look of classic 1970s dive watches with a distinctive and considerably more colorful design language. Among the many available colorways, the turquoise version is especially striking. Its vivid dial contrasts sharply with the black minute track and dark sapphire bezel insert. Hands and applied markers are generously coated with Super-LumiNova C3 X1, while the bezel markings use blue-emitting Super-LumiNova BGW9. Even the screw-down crown features a luminous marker. The fully brushed 40mm stainless-steel case measures 46mm from lug to lug, keeping the AquaSport II comfortably wearable despite its robust construction. A slightly domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating on both sides, a unidirectional bezel with a precise 120-click action, and water resistance to 200 meters reinforce its functional credentials. The watch is available on either a tropical rubber strap or a solid beads-of-rice steel bracelet with a quick-change system. Inside is the Swiss automatic Sellita SW200-1 in Elaboré grade. Circula regulates each movement in Pforzheim to a daily rate of -5 to +7 seconds. In addition to turquoise, the AquaSport II is regularly offered in blue, green, orange, yellow, red, brown, and gray, along with special editions such as the Original LE. Reference AE-ST-TS | Stainless steel 316L, 40mm | Caliber Sellita SW200-1 Elaboré, automatic | Power reserve: at least 38 hours | Water resistance: 200 meters | Approximately $1,000. This article was first published by WatchTime Germany.

title: Sheffield Introduces the $258 “Brian’s Sheffield” Chronograph
description: Sheffield has launched a 95-piece green-dial chronograph benefiting the Brian LaViolette Scholarship Foundation, with $100 from each sale donated.
content: Sheffield Introduces the $258 “Brian’s Sheffield” Chronograph Green, gold, and giving back Sheffield Watch Company has introduced the “Brian’s Sheffield” Chronograph, a 95-piece limited edition created to benefit the Brian LaViolette Scholarship Foundation. The chronograph collaboration grew out of an unlikely connection between two childhood watches, one belonging to Sheffield founder Jay Turkbas and the other to Brian LaViolette, whose family later established the foundation in his memory. For those unfamiliar with the watchmaker, Sheffield is a revived name with roots in the affordable watch market of the 1960s and early 1970s, when the original company sold inexpensive Swiss-made watches— including its likely best-known Allsport diver. The modern Sheffield was revived in 2023 by Jay Turkbas, whose connection to the brand dates to when his parents gave him a Sheffield Allsport dive watch at age 11, beginning a lifelong interest in watches. That first-watch story is also what connects Sheffield to Brian LaViolette. Brian received a Green Bay Packers watch from his parents at the age of four and developed an interest in watches and collecting of his own. After he died in a swimming accident at 15, his family established the Brian LaViolette Scholarship Foundation in his memory. The organization says it has since awarded more than 1,200 scholarships in the United States and abroad. The new chronograph brings those two stories together while benefiting the foundation directly. For every watch sold, Sheffield will contribute $100 to the Foundation’s endowment campaign. If all 95 watches sell, that will amount to $9,500. A Green Take on the Sheffield Chrono II The Brian’s Sheffield is based on the brand’s existing Chrono II, with a 42mm stainless-steel case, sapphire crystal with anti-glare coating, screw-down crown, and 100 meters of water resistance. Most of what separates this edition from the standard model is on the dial. Watch photographer Ty Alexander — a longtime supporter of the Foundation — developed the green-and-gold color scheme as a reference to Brian’s childhood Packers watch. The sunburst green dial is paired with two contrasting silver-toned subdials, applied baton markers, oversized Arabic numerals at 12 and 6, and a white tachymeter scale around the perimeter. Yellow-gold accents appear on the central chronograph seconds hand and the smaller counter hands. Sheffield branding sits below the 12 o’clock position, while the Brian LaViolette Scholarship Foundation logo appears in parallel above the 6 o’clock. Mecha-Quartz Inside Inside the watch is the Seiko VK64 mecha-quartz chronograph movement, a familiar choice in affordable chronographs. The quartz movement from Seiko measures 5.10mm thick and operates its central chronograph seconds hand in 1/5-second increments, with timing available up to 60 minutes. Accuracy is rated to ±20 seconds per month, with battery life of approximately three years. The appeal of the VK64 is its hybrid chronograph operation. Timekeeping is handled electronically, while the chronograph uses a mechanical module that gives the central seconds hand a smoother sweep and allows it to snap quickly back to zero when reset. It’s a well-established solution for keeping the watch affordable while giving the chronograph a little more tactile interest than a conventional quartz movement. Availability and Pricing The Sheffield “Brian’s Sheffield” Chronograph is limited to 95 pieces and is available now exclusively through Sheffield. The watch is priced at $258, with $100 from each sale contributed to the Brian LaViolette Scholarship Endowment Campaign.

title: The Seal of Approval: A Guide to the World of Watch Certifications and Quality Seals
description: Certifications and quality seals have long been used to safeguard reputations, certify precision, and communicate excellence in watchmaking. From chronometer standards to regional marks of distinction, here’s a look at what these credentials really mean — and why not every brand uses them.
content: The Seal of Approval: A Guide to the World of Watch Certifications and Quality Seals Chronometer-guaranteed Precision One of the best-known certifications for watches is that of a chronometer. About 15 percent of all watches exported out of Switzerland are chronometer certified. Brands like Rolex and Breitling certify their entire collection as a chronometer, making it an intricate part of their brand DNA and market proposition. This certification process is carried out at the Contrôle Officiel Suisse des Chronomètres, or COSC. The watch’s movement is tested in four phases according to ISO 3159 to become a chronometer. The entire cycle takes 15 days, in which the regularity of the movement is determined by varying both the temperature and the position. All this time, the performance of the individual movement is closely monitored, and when it remains within the set standards during testing, it will be awarded a chronometer certificate. The exact standards vary, as a difference is made between mechanical movements with a diameter smaller than 20 mm and those larger. Quartz movements can also be chronometer certified, but those have even more stringent criteria to meet. While COSC is the predominant chronometer institute in watchmaking, it is not the only one. Wempe has some of its watches chronometer certified at its observatory building in Glashütte, the only place in Germany where this is possible. The Observatory of Besançon, the heart of French watchmaking, is another place where a watch can be certified as a chronometer. Here, they test the precision of the final watch, so with the movement cased. In 16 days, the accuracy is tested in five different positions and at three different temperatures: 8°C, 23°C, and 38°C. When the average deviation is within -4 to +6 seconds, it is chronometer certified. In this case, it gets stamped with the observatory mark of the viper, also known as ‘Tête de Vipère.’ Mastering Precision In 2014, Omega launched, together with the Swiss Federal Institute for Metrology (METAS), an independent certification that takes the chronometer to the next level. Known as “Master Chronometer,” it takes a chronometer-certified movement and puts it through eight different tests focusing on resistance to magnetism, isochronism, power reserve, and water resistance. Its precision requirements are more strict, as to qualify, a watch must be able to function each day by gaining a maximum of 5 seconds. Losing time is not allowed, and the reason for that is that in the worst case, people will be somewhere slightly earlier than just a little bit late. When all passed, METAS will award the watch with the Master Chronometer certificate. While Omega is currently offering watches with this certification throughout its entire collection, other brands are also free to certify their watches. One brand that has already done so is Tudor. Its Black Bay Ceramic and Black Bay with burgundy bezel come with this certificate. Getting Regional Some quality seals are regional, meaning that for a watch to obtain them, it must be made in a specific area. Traditionally, they were established to safeguard the quality of production and promote the competitiveness of the regional manufacturers. While they still do that in a way, they are more prestigious signs of excellence. The most well-known is the Geneva Seal, also known as the ‘Hallmark of Geneva,’ or by its original French name, ‘Poinçon de Genève.’ It was founded in 1886 by the Canton of Geneva, which still governs it. To obtain it, the brand must be registered in the Canton of Geneva, where it should also carry out a large portion of the production and assembly of the watch, as well as the final inspection. Although there are some technical aspects to the Geneva Seal, most of them refer to the finishing. While the requirements are rather specific, it still offers enough room for brands to create watches that fit their DNA: for example, Vacheron Constantin uses the Geneva Seal, but so does Roger Dubuis. The town of Fleurier is also a Swiss hot spot for haute horlogerie. In 2001, Chopard, Bovet, and Parmigiani joined forces to create the Fleurier Quality Foundation (FQF). It focuses on various aspects, determined to deliver the best quality possible. While raw materials may come from abroad, everything else, from initial design to the watch’s manufacturing, assembly, and quality control, needs to be done in Switzerland. Next, there is a stringent set of aesthetic and technical criteria that the watches must meet, and one of them is that its movement is chronometer certified by COSC. This is followed by a Chronofiable aging test replicating the rigors of daily wear. This includes water and shock resistance, but also the effect of magnetic fields. Furthermore, it tests the operation of the crown and any of the push buttons, such as chronograph pushers and/or calendar correctors. Only then is the watch ready for its final test on the Fleuritest simulator. This advanced device performs a 24-hour operating test, and passing it will be the last hurdle for a watch to receive the ‘FQF, La Haute Horlogerie certifiée.’ Why Don’t They? Not all brands offer watches with certifications and/or quality seals from outside or independent organizations. The reasons for this can vary. Obtaining a chronometer certification costs time and money, making the watch inevitably more expensive than when it would come without one. As some popular movements, like Sellita’s SW200-1, have proven that they can meet chronometer standards, many brands using this caliber don’t go through the trouble of having them certified. Other brands have developed their own quality seals, often combined with a rigorous testing program. These are often brands that have already enjoyed an outstanding reputation for decades. Having their own quality programs allows them to be more dynamic in how and what they test and certify without interference from outside organizations, adding flexibility while maintaining the integrity of the brand. Jaeger-LeCoultre is famous for its 1,000-hour testing, while Montblanc also applies a similar 500-hour testing on the part of its collection. In 2009, Patek Philippe made the bold move to stop certifying its watches with the Geneva Seal in favor of its own quality seal. While this testing may not be (fully) independent, none of these brands will cut corners when it comes to certifying their timepieces. In fact, most have started developing their own testing protocols to be even more strict. Nearly all include precision testing of the movement when it is already cased, stringent quality control, set standards for finishing, and extensive simulation of daily wear, all to ensure that when the watch reaches the client, all expectations are met. While some brands are more vocal about this certification than others, it does not mean that they don’t exist. While certifications and quality seals confirm certain qualities within a watch, it doesn’t mean that timepieces without them don’t meet the same requirements. For some brands, it is a way to safeguard well-established reputations, while for others, it is another way of communicating the quality of their products with (potential) clients. This article was originally published in the March / April 2024 print issue. To subscribe to WatchTime Magazine, click here.

title: Chopard L.U.C Essence of Shunga: Swiss High Horolgy Meets Japanese Lacquer Art
description: A rotating display of Japanese Shunga art gives Chopard’s one-of-a-kind L.U.C creation a provocative twist on traditional haute horlogerie.
content: Chopard L.U.C Essence of Shunga: Swiss High Horolgy Meets Japanese Lacquer Art Unique piece for Time in Art With the L.U.C Essence of Shunga, Chopard presents a one-of-a-kind timepiece that brings an unusual artistic expression of Japanese heritage to the wrist. The watch was created exclusively for Art in Time, the Monaco-based gallery specializing in independent and artistic watchmaking, to mark the opening of its new boutique in Tokyo’s Ginza district. Its Grand-Feu enamel dial features scenes executed using the elaborate Urushi lacquer technique. Two traditional forms of craftsmanship therefore come together in a single timepiece, both requiring patience, precision, and a high degree of manual skill. At the same time, the watch reflects the cultural exchange between Switzerland and Japan. Six Scenes Revealed in Rotation Measuring 40mm in diameter and just 8.1mm thick, the case is crafted from Chopard’s 18-karat ethical rose gold. Behind the enamel dial, a rotating disc carries six erotic scenes executed in the traditional Urushi technique and inspired by Shunga art. The individual motifs gradually appear through an aperture in the upper part of the dial as the disc rotates. The term Shunga, which can be translated as “spring pictures,” refers to a form of erotic art that flourished particularly during Japan’s Edo period, from 1603 to 1868. Its imagery is not limited to eroticism, but also explores intimacy, relationships, beauty, and humor. Today, Shunga is recognized as an important part of Japan’s artistic heritage. The dial itself also incorporates elements of Japanese culture. Against its dark blue, shimmering background, pink-gold Japanese numerals and a stylized tea house stand out harmoniously. Manufacture Caliber with a 65-Hour Power Reserve A sapphire crystal caseback provides a view of the automatic L.U.C 96.29-L. Finished to the standards of Swiss watchmaking, the manufacture movement is equipped with a micro-rotor, which contributes to its slim profile. The L.U.C 96.29-L operates at a frequency of 28,800 vibrations per hour and provides a 65-hour power reserve. A One-of-a-Kind Creation for Art in Time The L.U.C Essence of Shunga was created exclusively for Art in Time and is limited to a single example. It is paired with a burgundy alligator leather strap and priced at €97,000, excluding VAT or approximately €97,000, excluding VAT or approximately $112,000 when converted to USD.

title: The Hermès Cape Cod Gets a Tougher, Sportier Makeover
description: Hermès sends the Cape Cod's signature design offshore, cuts loose the wraparound strap, and gains an in-house movement in the process.
content: The Hermès Cape Cod Gets a Tougher, Sportier Makeover A tougher take on one of Hermès’s most distinctive designs With the Hermès Cape Cod, the maison is pushing one of its oldest watch lines into new material territory: the model, designed by Henri d’Origny in 1991, is now available in a titanium version fitted with the maison’s own H1912 manufacture caliber. The new release marks a double shift — one in design, one in movement. From Saddle to Anchor Link Unlike many other Hermès watches, the Cape Cod owes nothing to the equestrian world so closely tied to the house’s heritage. Its form — a square within a rectangle — traces back to a link in the “Chaîne d’Ancre,” the anchor-chain motif that also appears throughout Hermès jewelry. The Cape Cod earned much of its fame through its double-wrapped leather strap, designed by Martin Margiela in 1998 during his tenure at Hermès, and still considered the line’s defining feature to this day. The new titanium version breaks with exactly that element: in place of the wraparound leather strap comes a quick-release rubber strap in black, blue, orange, or yellow. It’s a trade-off that strips away part of the Cape Cod’s traditional identity while granting it far greater versatility — one that suits this edition’s sportier direction. 41mm of Titanium, Finished Two Ways The case measures 41mm and wears two distinct finishes: satin-brushed on top, bead-blasted along the flanks. Together, they pull the Cape Cod noticeably away from the high-gloss look of earlier editions and toward something more technical in feel. The black dial reinforces that shift — its sandblasted center absorbs light, while the satin-brushed outer ring provides contrast and lends the face a sense of depth. The only splash of color comes from the orange seconds hand, which stands out deliberately against the monochrome backdrop. The applied Arabic numerals and baton hands are rhodium-plated and treated with Super-LumiNova, ensuring legibility day and night. Water resistance is rated to 10 bar. The H1912: A New Generation What’s happening under the dial is where things get technically interesting. The H1912 is an automatic mechanical caliber measuring 23.9mm in diameter and 3.9mm thick, running at 28,800 vibrations per hour, or 4 Hz, with a 45-hour power reserve. It’s manufactured by Vaucher Manufacture Fleurier, in which Hermès has held a 25 percent stake since 2006 — an early investment that gave the house a head start over other so-called “fashion brands”: Louis Vuitton didn’t acquire La Fabrique du Temps until 2011, and Chanel didn’t take a stake in Kenissi until 2019. Through Vaucher, Hermès sources movements that compete technically with those supplied to houses like Audemars Piguet or Richard Mille. The H1912 represents the second generation of movement within the Cape Cod line. The key difference: a free-sprung balance now replaces the Triovis regulating system — a detail that primarily improves long-term accuracy, since eliminating the regulator index reduces the interference that typically comes with adjustment. The caliber is visible through a titanium-framed sapphire crystal caseback, its bridges bearing the recurring H-motif that runs through Hermès movements. Where It Stands in the Market Priced at around $7,900, the Cape Cod Titanium undercuts comparable models like the Cartier Santos de Cartier LM in titanium or the Bulgari Octo Finissimo 37mm. Those rivals may offer more everyday versatility with their integrated bracelets, but the Cape Cod counters with a manufacture movement that holds its own on both price and technical merit. The Cape Cod Titanium reads less as a replacement for the existing line than as a reinterpretation built on more than three decades of design evolution — closer to an “offshore,” ruggedized companion piece than a successor. And the fact that Hermès chose to build it around its own manufacture caliber, rather than an outsourced base movement, says a great deal about how far the house has come as a serious watchmaker since its first move into Vaucher.

title: Bangalore Watch Company’s First Pocket Watch Looks Back to 1947
description: Inspired by the pivotal year of 1947, Bangalore Watch Company’s first-ever pocket watch combines mid-century design cues with a contemporary take on modern Indian history.
content: Bangalore Watch Company’s First Pocket Watch Looks Back to 1947 A pocket watch inspired by the beginning of modern India Pocket watches are a timeless classic for horological enthusiasts, but they are having a moment. The recent Swatch x Audemars Piguet Royal Oak pocket watch caused quite a stir in the watch world, bringing the traditional format back into the spotlight. Now Bangalore Watch Company is taking its own approach with the Forty-Seven, a pocket watch inspired by the formative years of modern India. Looking back to 1947 The Bangalore Watch Company has built its collections around stories from contemporary India, drawing on subjects including aviation, cricket, space exploration and the outdoors. The Forty-Seven takes a different perspective by going back to the starting point of that narrative. The period following independence was marked by ambitious efforts to build the foundations of a modern nation. At the time, India faced very different economic and social circumstances from those of today. The brand points to a literacy rate of around 12 percent, a per-capita income of approximately $50 and a country carrying significant debt. The decades that followed would see India develop into one of the world's largest and fastest-growing economies. That transformation is the historical backdrop for the Forty-Seven. Rather than celebrating the past for its own sake, Bangalore Watch Company says the timepiece is intended as a tribute to the generation that chose to focus on building the future. “Forty-Seven is a tribute to the years that shaped modern India. A pocket watch was the natural choice, because it belonged to that time,” says Nirupesh Joshi, co-founder of Bangalore Watch Company. “With this watch, the brand goes back to where those stories first began.” A Traditional Pocket-Watch Silhouette The 46mm case follows the proportions and design language of pocket watches from the first half of the 20th century. It is made from 316L surgical steel and finished with rose-gold PVD, giving it a warm appearance. The off-white dial has a linen-like texture and remains deliberately restrained, with the subsidiary seconds at 6 o'clock. The distinctive Arabic numerals, cathedral-style hour hand, and minute hand are coated with Swiss Superluminova, ensuring clear legibility even in the dark. The dial is protected by a K1 hardened crystal. A push-and-pull crown bearing the Bangalore Watch Company logo sits at the top of the case, while the closed case back can be personalized with an engraving, giving owners the option to add a personal message or inscription. Quartz Rather Than Nostalgia Inside, Forty-Seven uses a Swiss-made Ronda 6004.D quartz movement. It provides the straightforward three-hand display expected of a pocket watch and offers a battery life of approximately 40 months. The choice of quartz is notable in a product so closely tied to traditional watchmaking. Bangalore Watch Company has previously emphasized technical experimentation across its collections, including the use of recovered aircraft and aircraft-carrier materials, meteorites and captured carbon. With the Forty-Seven, the focus is less on mechanical complexity than on the object itself and the story it represents. Leather Lanyard and Rose-Gold Clip The traditional pocket-watch character continues with the attachment. The Forty-Seven comes with a lanyard-style genuine leather strap described by the brand as oil-pulled leather. A matching rose-gold-colored clip completes the ensemble and allows the watch to be carried in a pocket or attached to clothing. The Bangalore Watch Company Forty-Seven is priced at $1,250. (Discover more timepieces designed to be worn beyond the wrist.)

title: In a Farewell to Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer Launches Formula 1 Solargraph
description: For the final Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer introduces two limited-edition Formula 1 Solargraph models in a compact 38mm format.
content: In a Farewell to Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer Launches Formula 1 Solargraph Special edition of two limited series TAG Heuer marks the final Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Circuit Zandvoort, which will take place from 21 to 23 August 2026, with two new Formula 1 Solargraph limited editions. Limited to 1,500 and 1,000 pieces respectively, a distinguish by ones rubber strap and the other's steel bracelet, the watches combine a 38mm sandblasted steel case with a gray opaline dial, orange and red accents, and the Formula 1 collection’s bold design language. Both watches are powered by the brand's light-driven TH50-00 Solargraph movement. The choice of Zandvoort as the inspiration for the two watches reflects the circuit’s place in Formula 1 history and its distinctive setting on the Dutch coast. The track runs through the dunes and features tight sections and banked corners, while Formula 1’s return to the venue has become closely associated with the orange-clad crowds filling the grandstands to support Max Verstappen in a festival-like beachside setting. A Compact Formula 1 Case The two new models bring the Formula 1 collection back to a 38mm case size, echoing the proportions of earlier watches from the line when it was introduced in 1986. The sandblasted steel construction gives the case a matte surface, while the bidirectional TH-Polylight bezel features an orange 60-second/minute scale. A flat sapphire crystal with anti-reflective treatment protects the dial with bright orange and red accents inspired by the visual identity of Zandvoort and its distinctive racing atmosphere. Red lacquered applied indexes and hour and minute hands are filled with eggshell-colored Superluminova, which glows green in the dark. The central seconds hand and TAG Heuer logo are also rendered in red. Both versions feature a date display at 3 o’clock and are water-resistant to 100 meters. Two Versions, One Solargraph Movement The technical platform is the same for both editions, with each opting for the TAG Heuer’s TH50-00 quartz movement, which draws energy from both natural and artificial light. According to the brand, one minute of direct sunlight provides enough energy for approximately one day of operation. A full charge requires less than 40 hours of light exposure and provides up to ten months of autonomy in complete darkness. Should the watch stop, just ten seconds of exposure to light is sufficient to restart it. The accumulator is designed to last for up to 15 years. The first version, the reference WBY111H.FT8128, is limited to 1,500 pieces and comes with an orange rubber strap and steel pin buckle. The second, reference WBY111L.BA0042, is limited to 1,000 pieces and pairs the 38mm case with a three-row sandblasted steel bracelet. Its folding clasp features double safety push-buttons and an adjustment-link extension. Both will be available from this month and will retail for $2,150 and $2,250, respectively.

title: Seven of the Best Alternatives to the Rolex Submariner
description: The Rolex Submariner is the world’s most famous dive watch, but compelling alternatives from Omega, Tudor, TAG Heuer, and others range from accessible to decidedly luxurious.
content: Seven of the Best Alternatives to the Rolex Submariner Seven watches that offer their own take on the modern luxury diver The Rolex Submariner is the archetype of an entire watch category: the dive watch. For decades, it has set the benchmark for design, precision, reliability, durability, and legibility. At the same time, its sporty elegance has carried it far beyond the world of professional diving. Few watches combine brand prestige, desirability, instant recognition, and everyday versatility quite so effortlessly. Yet that very popularity makes the search for alternatives even more interesting. A high-quality dive watch does not have to be a Submariner. Some models come remarkably close in terms of status, specifications, and price. Others take a more individual approach — more technical, more historically driven, more elegant, or considerably more affordable. Our selection therefore ranges from high-end manufacture pieces and accomplished Swiss sports watches to attractive entry-level models with automatic movements and 300 meters of water resistance. The goal was not to find watches that simply look like the Submariner. Instead, we focused on models capable of fulfilling a similar role: robust, versatile, and equally suited to everyday wear, travel, and water. Omega Seamaster Diver 300M The Omega Seamaster Diver 300M is arguably the most prominent alternative to the Rolex Submariner. Since its introduction in 1993, the collection has become one of Omega’s most important sports-watch lines, combining genuine diving capability with a strong presence on the wrist. Its James Bond connection helped make it famous. For anyone seeking a luxury dive watch that combines advanced mechanics, Swiss watchmaking heritage, and a touch of pop culture, the Seamaster makes a compelling case. At 42mm, it is slightly larger than the Submariner, but it likewise offers 300 meters of water resistance and a unidirectional dive bezel. One of its defining differences is the dial, with its distinctive wave pattern, along with the characteristically scalloped bezel that gives the Seamaster Diver 300M an unmistakable visual identity. Omega’s strongest argument, however, may be the movement. The Co-Axial Master Chronometer caliber 8806 is METAS-certified, offers a 55-hour power reserve, and resists magnetic fields up to 15,000 gauss. The Omega is also equipped with a helium escape valve at 10 o’clock, reinforcing its credentials as a professional dive watch. For anyone looking for a high-end diver from a major brand, backed by strong history and a design language entirely its own, the Seamaster Diver 300M remains one of the most convincing alternatives to the Rolex Submariner. Reference 210.30.42.20.01.010 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Omega Co-Axial Master Chronometer caliber 8806, automatic | 55-hour power reserve | Approximately $8,100 Tudor Black Bay 58 The Tudor Black Bay 58 is one of the most obvious alternatives to the Rolex Submariner, because Tudor has not only long-standing historical ties to Rolex but also a distinguished dive-watch heritage of its own. Its name refers to 1958, the year Tudor introduced Ref. 7924, a dive watch water-resistant to 200 meters. That combination of heritage, robust engineering, and wearable proportions is precisely what makes the Black Bay 58 so appealing. At 39mm, it is more compact than many modern sports watches. Its three-link steel bracelet, with distinctive rivet-style detailing, also has a more individual character than Rolex’s familiar Oyster bracelet. Compared with the Submariner, however, the Black Bay is less status-driven. Its design is more understated and carries a subtle retro character, thanks to Tudor’s signature Snowflake hour hand, first introduced in 1969. It is also considerably more accessible in price. Inside is the manufacture caliber MT5400-U. The movement is certified by both COSC and METAS, features a silicon balance spring, and offers a 65-hour power reserve. Reference M7939A1A0NU-0002 | Stainless steel, 39mm | 200 meters of water resistance | Manufacture caliber MT5400-U, automatic | 65-hour power reserve | Approximately $5,600 TAG Heuer Aquaracer Professional 300 Date The TAG Heuer Aquaracer Professional 300 Date is one of the strongest Submariner alternatives in the mid-luxury segment. It delivers nearly everything expected of a modern dive watch: a robust stainless-steel case, 300 meters of water resistance, a screw-down crown, sapphire crystal, ceramic bezel, and a solid steel bracelet with a safety folding clasp. At the same time, it looks markedly more angular and technical than the Rolex, particularly with its 12-sided bezel, blue wave-pattern dial, and orange seconds hand. TAG Heuer has steadily refined the Aquaracer in recent years, and its greatest strength now lies in its specifications. The current Professional 300 Date is powered by the COSC-certified TH31-00 caliber, produced by Sellita’s AMT manufacture division, and offers an impressive 80-hour power reserve. Despite its 42mm diameter, the watch remains comparatively slim at 12mm thick. For anyone seeking a distinctive, robust Swiss dive watch with a chronometer-certified movement, the Aquaracer Professional 300 Date is a particularly compelling and rational alternative. Reference WBP5111.BA0013 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Caliber TH31-00 COSC, automatic, AMT/Sellita | 80-hour power reserve | Approximately $5,200 Longines HydroConquest The Longines HydroConquest is an insider tip for anyone seeking a high-quality Swiss dive watch without stepping into high-end luxury territory. Compared with the Submariner, it feels more contemporary and is considerably more accessible in price. Its unidirectional ceramic bezel, prominently styled minute hand, and excellent legibility in low light and underwater give it the unmistakable character of a purpose-built diver. Water resistance to 300 meters reinforces those credentials. The 39mm version, in particular, combines the robustness of a full-fledged dive watch with compact, contemporary proportions, making it equally suitable for everyday wear, travel, and more active use. Inside is a modern automatic movement produced exclusively for Longines by ETA, its sister company within the Swatch Group. It offers an impressive power reserve of up to 72 hours. For anyone looking for strong value in a Swiss mechanical dive watch, the HydroConquest deserves serious consideration. Reference L3.779.4.56.6 | Stainless steel, 39mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Longines caliber L888.5, automatic | Approximately 72-hour power reserve | Approximately $2,500 Breitling Superocean Heritage B31 Automatic 42 The Breitling Superocean Heritage B31 Automatic 42 is an appealing Submariner alternative for anyone drawn to a major brand with a strong history and a more individual sense of elegance. The model traces its roots to the original Superocean of 1957, a watch conceived not merely as a professional diving instrument, but as a stylish sports watch in its own right. The 42mm stainless-steel model remains a fully capable dive watch, with a unidirectional bezel featuring a ceramic insert, a screw-down crown, and water resistance to 200 meters. Its distinctive character comes from the arrow-shaped hour hand, spear-shaped minute hand, unconventional hour markers, and domed sapphire crystal. Together, these details reflect Breitling’s “modern retro” design philosophy. Power comes from the automatic three-hand caliber B31. The movement is chronometer-certified and delivers approximately 78 hours of power reserve. Reference AB3111241B1A1 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 200 meters of water resistance | Manufacture caliber B31, automatic | COSC-certified chronometer | Approximately 78-hour power reserve | Approximately $7,700 Tissot: Seastar 1000 Powermatic 80 For anyone seeking a particularly affordable dive watch with plenty to offer both technically and visually, Tissot makes a strong case. The Seastar 1000 Powermatic 80 does not pretend to compete with the Rolex Submariner in status or finishing, but it delivers many of the features expected of a modern dive watch. Its 40mm stainless-steel case is fitted with a sapphire crystal, screw-down crown, screw-down caseback, unidirectional bezel, and 300 meters of water resistance. As part of the Swatch Group, Tissot is one of the best-known Swiss brands in the entry-level mechanical segment, and the Seastar benefits from that position. It feels sporty, well made, and thoroughly practical while remaining far more affordable than traditional luxury divers. A black dial, bold hands and markers with Super-LumiNova, and a steel bracelet with a quick-release system make it an easy choice for everyday wear, travel, and time in the water. The movement is another strong point: the Powermatic 80 delivers up to 80 hours of power reserve and features an antimagnetic Nivachron hairspring. Reference T120.807.11.051.00 | Stainless steel, 40mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Powermatic 80, automatic, based on ETA C.07 | Up to 80-hour power reserve | Approximately $900 Glashütte Original SeaQ Panorama Date The Glashütte Original SeaQ Panorama Date is one of the most compelling alternatives to the Rolex Submariner for buyers who value not only dive-watch capability, but also manufacture pedigree and a distinct sense of origin. Part of Glashütte Original’s Spezialist collection, the SeaQ traces its lineage to the Spezimatic Type RP TS 200 of 1969, giving it a genuine German dive-watch heritage of its own. Its 43.2mm stainless-steel case, unidirectional ceramic bezel, screw-down crown, sapphire crystal, and 300 meters of water resistance meet the essential requirements of a professional dive watch. Compared with the Submariner, the SeaQ is larger and more assertive on the wrist. It also adds a useful and visually distinctive complication: the brand’s Panorama Date at 4 o’clock. Inside is the manufacture caliber 36-13. Its architecture includes the traditional Glashütte three-quarter plate, while technical features include a 100-hour power reserve and a silicon balance spring. Finishing is equally elaborate, with beveled edges, Glashütte ribbing, and a skeletonized rotor fitted with a 21-karat gold oscillating weight. For anyone looking for a luxury dive watch with strong brand identity, serious technical substance, and unmistakable German manufacture character, the SeaQ Panorama Date is a particularly distinctive alternative to the Submariner.
